etymology: Text-speak initialism for the spoken oath I swear to God, an English intensifier long used far below its weight. The abbreviation circulated in chat rooms and early texting in the 2000s and became a staple of tweets, captions, and group chats through the 2010s; on TikTok it is typed lowercase at the front of a complaint, a threat, or a claim ("istg if he’s late again"). Shrinking the phrase made it feel weightless: a teen who would never say the full sentence at the dinner table will type the four letters a dozen times a day.
biblical_def: In current slang ISTG is an intensifier. It marks frustration ("istg this Wi-Fi"), a threat ("istg if you tell her"), or a claim the speaker wants believed ("istg I did my homework"). Spelled out, it is an oath on the name of God, made over nothing. The Christian observation: Scripture does not treat God’s name as punctuation. The third commandment stands over every keyboard: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain" (Exo 20:7). Lawful oaths exist — Israel was told to "swear by his name" (Deu 6:13) in solemn matters, and the Westminster Confession (ch. 22) keeps the oath for court and covenant — but our Lord forbids the casual oath that props up ordinary speech: "Swear not at all" (Mat 5:34); "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil" (Mat 5:37). James repeats it "above all things" (Jas 5:12). Notice the logic. A person who must say "I swear" to be believed is admitting his plain word is not enough, and the habit trains the conscience to keep two kinds of speech, sworn and unsworn. Peter, cornered by a servant girl, "began he to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man" (Mat 26:74) — the oath came out exactly when the truth did not. A father tells his son: let your yes be so reliable that you never need God’s name to hold it up, and keep that Name for prayer, praise, and the vows you will one day make before Him.
webster_summary: Gen-Z text-speak (2000s texting; everywhere online since the 2010s) abbreviating the oath "I swear to God," used as a casual intensifier — the vain use of the Name in four letters, which Christ answers with a plain yea and nay.
webster_full: ISTG, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2005–present; texting and social media) "I swear to God"; an intensifier marking exasperation, a threat, or a claim to be believed. "Istg if you post that picture."
Typed lowercase (istg) at the front of a sentence; spoken aloud as the full phrase or clipped to "I swear." Close kin to no cap and deadass, which do the same work without the Name.
Older senses a grandparent will know: to swear as taking a solemn oath in court, and to swear as using profane language; "I swear to God" belongs to the first and is misused as the second.

Webster (1828), root word swear: “SWEAR, verb intransitive preterit tense swore. […] 1. To affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed. Ye shall not swear by my name falsely. Leviticus 19:12. But I say unto you, swear not at all. Matthew 5:34. 2. To promise upon oath. Jacob said, swear to me this day;”
Decode for parents: your child is invoking God’s name as an exclamation mark, usually without noticing it is a name at all.
scriptures: Exo 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
Deu 6:13
Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and serve him, and shalt swear by his name.
Mat 5:34
But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Jas 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
corruption_summary: ISTG shrinks an oath on the name of God to four letters and spends it on Wi-Fi and homework, training a conscience that keeps sworn and unsworn speech apart.
corruption_paragraphs: An oath was once the heaviest sentence a man could say. To swear by God was to call Him as witness and judge, which is why Israel was told to swear only by His name and only in earnest (Deu 6:13), and why the man of Psalm 15 "sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not" (Psa 15:4). The abbreviation does the opposite. By shrinking the oath to four lowercase letters, it removes even the small hesitation a person felt in saying the Name aloud. The commandment against vain use (Exo 20:7) was not written for open blasphemers only; it was written for anyone who makes the Name light, and nothing is lighter than a typing shortcut.

Jesus goes further than the letter. The scribes of His day kept elaborate rules about which oaths bound and which did not — by the temple, by the gold of the temple, by heaven (Mat 23:16–22) — and He swept the whole system away: "Swear not at all" (Mat 5:34). His point is not that the courtroom oath is sin (the Reformed churches have always held that it is not), but that a disciple’s ordinary word should need no reinforcement. Peter’s worst hour came wrapped in oaths (Mat 26:72–74). Teach your children the cure: a plain yea, a plain nay, and a name for keeping them (Jas 5:12).
roots_summary: Old English swerian (to take an oath) → "I swear to God" as a spoken intensifier → 2000s texting ISTG → 2010s–2020s captions and group chats.
roots_lines: Old English swerian — to take an oath, to affirm with an appeal to God
Biblical oath formula: "as the LORD liveth" (1Sa 14:39) — solemn, rare, binding
Modern English "I swear to God" — a spoken intensifier, the oath emptied of its weight
2000s texting and chat: initialism ISTG
2010s–2020s Twitter, TikTok, and group chats: typed lowercase, many times a day
usage: "istg if Mr. Davis gives us another pop quiz I’m done."
Let your yea be yea, and your nay, nay (Jas 5:12) — no oath required.
God’s name is for prayer and praise, not punctuation (Exo 20:7).

etymology: Text abbreviation of not gonna lie ("not going to lie"), a spoken American hedge that grew common in the 2000s as a softener before an admission or an opinion ("not gonna lie, I cried"). The initialism ngl spread on Twitter and Tumblr in the early 2010s and became a TikTok and group-chat staple c. 2018–2020.
biblical_def: In current slang ngl introduces a mild confession or an honest opinion: "ngl that movie was mid," "ngl I’m kind of nervous." It works like a raised hand: what follows is unvarnished. Most of the time it is harmless, and sometimes it opens real candour between friends. The Christian observation: the phrase carries a quiet assumption — that without the label, lying would be on the table. For a believer there should be no gear change between ordinary speech and honest speech. "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another" (Eph 4:25). "Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds" (Col 3:9). Paul defended his own word on exactly this ground: "as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay" (2Co 1:18). The man who may dwell on God’s holy hill "speaketh the truth in his heart" (Psa 15:2) — not only in the sentences flagged as honest. Solomon makes no exception for the small social lie: "Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight" (Pro 12:22). And beneath all of it stands Christ, who said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Joh 14:6); His people tell the truth because they belong to the Truth. A father tells his daughter: use the phrase if you like, but live so that it is redundant — so that everyone who knows you assumes you are not lying, because you never do.
webster_summary: Gen-Z text-speak (spoken 2000s; ngl online 2010s–present) for "not gonna lie," a softener before a confession or opinion — harmless in use, but a reminder that a Christian’s every word should already be true.
webster_full: NGL, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2010–present; spoken form earlier) "Not gonna lie"; introduces a frank opinion or small confession. "Ngl I kind of liked the old version better."
Placed at the start or end of a sentence: "that test was hard ngl." Spoken in full as "not gonna lie" or "I’m not gonna lie." Close kin to tbh.
Older relatives a grandparent will know: "to tell you the truth," "honestly," "I’ll be frank" — the same hedge in older dress.

Webster (1828), root word lie: “LIE, noun 1. A criminal falsehood; a falsehood uttered for the purpose of deception; an intentional violation of truth. Fiction, or a false statement or representation, not intended to deceive, mislead or injure, as in fables, parables and the like, is not a lie It is willful deceit that makes a lie A man may act a lie as by pointing his …”
Decode for parents: usually a harmless softener; listen for whether your child treats honesty as a special occasion.
scriptures: Eph 4:25
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
Col 3:9
Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds;
But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay.
Psa 15:2
He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart.
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
corruption_summary: NGL is a harmless softener on its face, but it quietly sorts speech into flagged-honest and unflagged, when Scripture asks for one kind only.
corruption_paragraphs: Most uses of ngl are innocent; a teen admitting he cried at a film is not sinning by prefacing it. The trouble is the habit of mind the phrase can grow. If honesty needs announcing, then the default must be something less — the polite fib, the exaggeration, the story shaded to look better. A generation raised online has learned that every post is curated, and ngl becomes the small label on the rare unfiltered sentence. That is backwards. The believer has "put off the old man with his deeds" (Col 3:9), and lying is one of the garments that came off with him.

Paul was accused of being a man whose word shifted — yes today, no tomorrow — and his defence was theological: "as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay" (2Co 1:18). The faithfulness of God is the ground of a Christian’s plain speech. We do not tell the truth because a phrase warns that we are about to; we tell it because we are "members one of another" (Eph 4:25) and belong to the God who cannot lie. Let your children say ngl if they like; teach them that for a Christian it should always be true already.
roots_summary: Old English leogan (to lie) → spoken hedge "not gonna lie" (2000s) → ngl on Twitter and Tumblr (early 2010s) → TikTok and texting staple.
roots_lines: Old English leogan — to tell a falsehood
Older hedges: "to tell the truth," "honestly," "frankly"
2000s American speech: "not gonna lie" before a confession or opinion
Early 2010s: initialism ngl on Twitter and Tumblr
c. 2018–present: TikTok captions and group chats
usage: "ngl I was lowkey scared on that ride."
Speak every man truth with his neighbour (Eph 4:25) — flagged or not.
A Christian’s word is not yea and nay (2Co 1:18); honesty is the default, not the exception.

etymology: Text abbreviation of to be honest, a long-standing English hedge. The initialism appears in internet forums and chat by the 2000s. c. 2013–2015 it became a teen social-media ritual on Instagram and Facebook ("like for a tbh"), in which each friend who liked a post received a short public verdict on themselves from the poster. In 2017 an anonymous-compliment app named tbh topped the app charts and was bought by Facebook. Now a general softener in speech and text.
biblical_def: In current slang tbh prefixes an honest opinion, often one the hearer may not like: "tbh I don’t think he’s good for you," or simply "tbh I’m tired." In the mid-2010s it was also a game: like a post and receive a public "tbh" rating from the poster. The Christian observation: honesty is a virtue Scripture commands, and Scripture also tells us what honesty is for. "Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour" (Zec 8:16) — and Paul adds the manner and the aim: "speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ" (Eph 4:15). Honest words are meant to build a brother up toward Christ, not to win the room. Proverbs honours the hard word: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Pro 27:6), and the rebuker "shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue" (Pro 28:23). Yet a sentence can be true and still cruel, and the old "tbh" posts often were — frankness as a licence for a public put-down. The honesty God wants starts further in: "thou desirest truth in the inward parts" (Psa 51:6), a person honest with God about himself before he is honest with anyone else. A father tells his son: be the friend who tells the truth when it costs him; say it to the person and not about him; and say it in a way that leaves him nearer to Christ.
webster_summary: Gen-Z text-speak (2000s chat; teen social-media ritual c. 2013–2015) for "to be honest" — a frankness Scripture commends when it is spoken in love to build a brother up toward Christ.
webster_full: TBH, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2005–present; chat and social media) "To be honest"; introduces a frank opinion. "Tbh I liked the first one better."
c. 2013–2015: a social-media game, "like for a tbh," in which the poster gave each liker a short public opinion of them; also the name of a 2017 anonymous-compliment app.
Older relatives a grandparent will know: "to be honest with you," "frankly," "candidly."

Webster (1828), root word truth: “TRUTH, noun 1. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be. The truth of history constitutes its whole value. We rely on the truth of the scriptural prophecies. My mouth shall speak truth Proverbs 8:7. Sanctify them through thy truth; thy word is truth John 17:17. 2.”
Decode for parents: usually a softener; when it introduces a verdict on another person, ask whether it was said to them or about them.
scriptures: Zec 8:16
These are the things that ye shall do; Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates:
Eph 4:15
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue.
Psa 51:6
Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.
corruption_summary: TBH prizes frankness, which Scripture also prizes, but detaches it from love and from self-examination, so that honesty can become a licence for a public put-down.
corruption_paragraphs: There is something right in a generation that wants people to be real. Scripture is full of hard, honest speech — Nathan before David, Paul withstanding Peter to the face — and it calls the friend who wounds faithfully better than the enemy who kisses (Pro 27:6). A teen who will tell his friend "tbh you’re drifting" may be doing him the greatest kindness of the year. Flattery is the commoner sin, and Proverbs promises that the honest rebuker ends with "more favour" than the flatterer (Pro 28:23).

The corruption is honesty cut loose from its purpose. The mid-2010s "tbh" posts often handed out public ratings — "tbh you’re kind of fake" — under cover of candour. Paul does not say merely "speak the truth"; he says "speaking the truth in love" and gives the goal, that we "grow up into him in all things" (Eph 4:15). Honest words aimed at Christ are medicine; honest words aimed at an audience are often cruelty in a clean shirt. And honesty begins at home: "thou desirest truth in the inward parts" (Psa 51:6). The friend who is honest about his own sin is the one whose honesty about yours can be trusted.
roots_summary: Old English treowth (faithfulness, truth) → "to be honest" as a hedge → tbh in 2000s chat → c. 2013–2015 "like for a tbh" → general softener.
roots_lines: Old English treowth — faithfulness, pledged loyalty, truth
Latin honestus — honourable; English honest, upright and truthful
2000s forums and chat: initialism tbh
c. 2013–2015 Instagram and Facebook: "like for a tbh" ratings; 2017 tbh app
Now a softener in speech and text, kin to ngl
usage: "tbh I don’t think you should go to that party."
Speak the truth in love, aiming at Christ (Eph 4:15).
Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6) — say it to him, not about him.

etymology: Abbreviation of if you know, you know, an American phrase for a reference only insiders will catch — an in-joke, a local spot, a shared memory. The full phrase was common in American speech by the 2000s; the initialism spread on Twitter and Instagram in the late 2010s and became a TikTok caption fixture c. 2020, attached to posts deliberately left unexplained.
biblical_def: In current slang iykyk tags something only insiders will understand: a photo of a school hallway, a song from summer camp, a meme with no explanation. Those who get it feel the warm glow of belonging; those who don’t are, by design, left outside. Much of it is harmless — every family has its jokes. The Christian observation: the gospel is the opposite of an in-joke. Christ said, "I spake openly to the world" and "in secret have I said nothing" (Joh 18:20), and He commanded the reverse of a secret: "what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops" (Mat 10:27). There are real mysteries in Scripture, but a Bible mystery is a secret God has now made known, not one hoarded by a clique: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deu 29:29). The early church fought a heresy, Gnosticism, built on exactly the iykyk instinct: salvation by secret knowledge for an enlightened few. Paul answered that in Christ "are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 2:3), and that "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1Co 8:1). The knowledge that saves is open to any sinner who asks: "this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent" (Joh 17:3). A father tells his daughter: enjoy your friends’ jokes, but never make being in the know the prize; and when it comes to Christ, you are the one who explains, to everyone, for free.
webster_summary: Gen-Z text-speak (phrase 2000s; initialism late 2010s, TikTok c. 2020–present) for "if you know, you know," tagging an insider reference — a harmless in-joke at best, and at worst the clique instinct the gospel overturns by preaching on the housetops.
webster_full: IYKYK, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2018–present; Twitter, Instagram, TikTok) "If you know, you know"; marks a reference only insiders will understand. "Third-period lunch table. Iykyk."
Used as a caption left deliberately unexplained; also spoken in full, often with a knowing look. Cousin: "you had to be there."
Older relatives a grandparent will know: the inside joke, the secret handshake, "those who know, know."

Webster (1828), root word know: “KNOW, verb transitive no. preterit tense knew; participle passive known. […] 1. To perceive with certainty; to understand clearly; to have a clear and certain perception of truth, fact, or any thing that actually exists. To know a thing pre includes all doubt or uncertainty of its existence.”
Decode for parents: mostly harmless in-jokes; watch for when a phrase like this is used to keep a particular child outside.
scriptures: Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing.
What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops.
The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Joh 17:3
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
corruption_summary: IYKYK makes belonging out of what others do not know — the old clique instinct, which the gospel reverses by publishing God’s secret to all.
corruption_paragraphs: Every circle has its private language, and a family that laughs at its own old jokes is a good thing. The danger in iykyk is that it turns that pleasure into a sorting tool. The point of the caption is that some will not know, and their not knowing is part of the fun. Schoolyards run on this; so did the ancient mystery cults, whose initiates were sworn to silence, and the Gnostic teachers who troubled the early church with a salvation for those who held the secret. "Knowledge puffeth up" (1Co 8:1) is Paul’s verdict on any knowledge used to stand above a brother.

Christ’s way is the reverse. He taught "openly to the world" (Joh 18:20) and sent His disciples to proclaim from the housetops what He had told them in the ear (Mat 10:27). Even the mysteries of Scripture are mysteries revealed — once hidden, now published to every nation, and "those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deu 29:29). The Christian who knows the Lord is not an insider guarding a password but a messenger sent to tell everyone. Teach your children to notice the kid who does not get the joke, and to explain the gospel to anyone willing to hear it.
roots_summary: Old English cnawan (to know) → "if you know, you know" (American speech) → iykyk late 2010s → TikTok caption c. 2020.
roots_lines: Old English cnawan — to perceive, recognise, know
Greek gnosis — knowledge; the root of the Gnostic heresy of secret saving knowledge
American speech, 2000s: "if you know, you know" for an insider reference
Late 2010s Twitter and Instagram: initialism iykyk
c. 2020–present: TikTok captions left deliberately unexplained
usage: "Mrs. Patterson’s substitute plans. Iykyk."
What ye hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops (Mat 10:27).
Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1Co 8:1) — explain the joke to the one left out.

etymology: Text abbreviation of at this point, used to signal that a situation has gone on so long, or so badly, that the speaker has reached a conclusion — usually an exasperated one ("atp just cancel the game"). The initialism spread on Twitter and TikTok c. 2019–2021. It collides with older initialisms: biology students know ATP as adenosine triphosphate, and sports fans know it as the men’s professional tennis tour.
biblical_def: In current slang atp marks a verdict reached after too much: "atp I’m just going to fail this class," "atp she’s not even trying." It is the sound of someone giving up with a shrug, sometimes funny, sometimes bitter. The Christian observation: the letters are harmless; the mood they often carry is not small. "At this point" is the voice of weariness deciding that what has been is what will be. Scripture speaks to that voice directly. "Let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not" (Gal 6:9). Jeremiah wrote Lamentations from the rubble of Jerusalem, at the lowest point a man could reach, and still confessed that the LORD’s "compassions fail not" (Lam 3:22): "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness" (Lam 3:23). Paul, pressed on every side, could write that he was "perplexed, but not in despair" (2Co 4:8). The believer’s "at this point" is never the last point, because God has not finished. "They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles" (Isa 40:31). There is a right kind of conclusion — changing a plan that is plainly not working is often wisdom — and a wrong kind, which is deciding that God’s promises have run out. A father tells his son: you may be tired, and you may need to change course, but never let a hard week write the verdict on your life; at this point, and at every point, the Lord is still at work.
webster_summary: Gen-Z text-speak (c. 2019–present) for "at this point," marking an exasperated conclusion — harmless in itself, though it often voices a weariness Scripture meets with mercies new every morning.
webster_full: ATP, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2019–present; Twitter, TikTok, texting) "At this point"; signals a conclusion reached after too much of something. "Atp I’m just going to sleep in the car."
Often begins a resigned or sarcastic verdict: "atp he should just apologize," "atp it’s embarrassing."
Older senses a grandparent will know: in biology, ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the molecule that carries energy in living cells; in sport, the Association of Tennis Professionals.

Webster (1828), root word point: “POINT, noun […] 1. The sharp end of any instrument or body; as the point of a knife, of a sword or of a thorn. 2. A string with a tag; as a silken point 3. A small cape, headland or promontory; a tract of land extending into the sea, a lake or river, beyond the line of the shore, and becoming narrow at the end; as point Judith;”
Decode for parents: a harmless abbreviation; listen for whether it is a joke or a child quietly giving up.
scriptures: Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Lam 3:22
It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
Lam 3:23
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
corruption_summary: ATP is a neutral abbreviation that often carries resignation — weariness deciding the future from the past — which Scripture answers with God’s faithfulness in due season.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with the letters. Sometimes "at this point" is plain good sense: the bus is not coming, call home. But the phrase is often the way a young person narrates surrender — to a class, a friendship, a sin he has stopped fighting. "Atp I’m just like this." The world encourages that shrug and calls it accepting yourself. Scripture calls it fainting, and warns against it, because the harvest comes "in due season" only to those who "faint not" (Gal 6:9).

The cure is not a pep talk but a Person. Lamentations is the Bible’s book of "at this point" — city burned, temple gone, the poet sitting in the ashes — and at its centre stands the confession that God’s compassions "are new every morning" (Lam 3:23). Paul could be "perplexed, but not in despair" (2Co 4:8) because his hope did not rest on how the week had gone. Teach your children the difference between changing course, which is often wisdom, and giving up on God’s promises, which never is.
roots_summary: Latin punctum (a prick, a dot) → English point → "at this point" (at this stage) → atp online c. 2019–2021.
roots_lines: Latin punctum, from pungo, to prick — a dot, a mark
English point — a place or a moment in a process
"At this point" — at this stage of affairs; often impatient
c. 2019–2021 Twitter and TikTok: atp as a resigned or sarcastic verdict
usage: "atp I’m not even mad, I’m just tired."
Let us not be weary in well doing (Gal 6:9).
His compassions fail not; they are new every morning (Lam 3:22–23).

etymology: Contracted from Southern American fixing to ("fixin’ to"), meaning about to or preparing to, long attested in Southern speech (19th century and earlier). African American Vernacular English shortened it to finna (also fitna, finta), and hip-hop carried it nationwide; it became common on Black Twitter and Vine c. 2013–2016 and is now ordinary Gen-Z speech and text.
biblical_def: In current slang finna means "about to": "I’m finna eat," "we finna leave." It is a Southern grandmother’s "fixin’ to" in a teenager’s mouth, and as speech it is perfectly innocent. The Christian observation: finna lives in the gap between intention and action, and Scripture has a good deal to say about that gap. Jesus told of a son who answered his father, "I go, sir: and went not" (Mat 21:30) — a young man perpetually finna. "In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury" (Pro 14:23). And James warns those who announce their plans as if tomorrow were theirs: "ye know not what shall be on the morrow" (Jas 4:14); "For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that" (Jas 4:15). Our grandparents had the right instinct when they added "Lord willing" to a plan. So the word teaches two lessons. First, do what you say you are about to do: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). Second, hold every plan with an open hand, because the next hour belongs to God. And the most important thing anyone can be "about to" do is repent and believe, which will not keep: "behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2Co 6:2). A father tells his son: don’t be finna obey — obey; and say "if the Lord will" over every plan you make.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (Southern fixing to, shortened in AAVE; mainstream online 2010s–present) for "about to" — innocent speech that names the gap between intention and obedience, and the "if the Lord will" every plan needs.
webster_full: FINNA, aux. v. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2013–present online; Southern and AAVE origin) About to; going to; preparing to. "I’m finna head out."
Variants fitna, finta. "Not finna" — a refusal: "I’m not finna argue with you."
Older form a grandparent will know: Southern "fixin’ to" — "I’m fixin’ to go to the store."

Webster (1828), root word fix: “FIX, verb transitive […] 1. To make stable; to set or establish immovably. The universe is governed by fixed laws. 2. To set or place permanently; to establish. The prince fixed his residence at York. The seat of our government is fixed at Washington in the district of Columbia. Some men have no fixed opinions. 3. To make fast;”
Decode for parents: completely innocent; your Southern relatives have said it for generations in longer form.
scriptures: And he came to the second, and said likewise. And he answered and said, I go, sir: and went not.
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
Jas 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
Jas 4:15
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
corruption_summary: Finna is harmless speech; the only corruption it can carry is the old one of living permanently "about to" — promising obedience and planning tomorrow without God.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing is wrong with a regional contraction. Tyndale wanted the ploughboy to know the Scriptures in his own tongue, and finna is as honest a piece of English as "gonna." If there is a danger, it is the one the word describes: a life lived in the future tense. The second son in Christ’s parable never defied his father; he simply said "I go, sir" and stayed put (Mat 21:30). Teenagers are experts at this — finna start the essay, finna call Grandma, finna read my Bible — and Proverbs keeps the ledger: talk of the lips "tendeth only to penury" (Pro 14:23).

The other danger runs the opposite way: plans spoken as though tomorrow were in our pocket. James is blunt with the merchant who says he will go to such a city and get gain: your life "is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away" (Jas 4:14). The Christian answer is not to stop planning but to plan under God — "If the Lord will" (Jas 4:15) — and then to do the next duty with might (Ecc 9:10). Teach your children both halves: keep your word quickly, and hold your tomorrow loosely.
roots_summary: Latin figo (to fasten) → English fix → Southern "fixing to" (preparing to) → AAVE finna → 2010s Black Twitter and Vine → general Gen-Z speech.
roots_lines: Latin figo, fixus — to fasten, to make fast
English fix — to settle, to prepare, to arrange
Southern American "fixing to" — about to, preparing to
African American Vernacular English: finna, fitna
2010s Black Twitter, Vine, and hip-hop → ordinary teen speech nationwide
usage: "I’m finna go to the gym after school."
Don’t be the son who said "I go, sir: and went not" (Mat 21:30).
Plan under God: if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that (Jas 4:15).

etymology: From English twin, one of two born at a birth. Twinning — two friends dressing or acting alike, usually in a matching photo — spread on social media in the 2010s. In the early 2020s twin became a term of address for a close friend ("what’s good, twin"), rising out of hip-hop and Black American speech and then through TikTok c. 2022–2023, where it is also used approvingly of anyone who shares your taste or opinion ("twin, we’re the same").
biblical_def: In current slang twin is a close friend, the one so like you that you might have shared a womb: "that’s my twin," or as an address, "you good, twin?" Twinning is dressing alike or thinking alike. It is a warm word, and much of the time it is simple affection. The Christian observation: Scripture’s most famous twins were not friends. "Behold, there were twins in her womb" (Gen 25:24), and Jacob and Esau struggled before they were born and for decades after; sameness of birth did not make sameness of heart. Real friendship in the Bible is a knitting of souls — "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (1Sa 18:1) — and two very different men can be knit closer than twins. The slang tends to prize the friend who mirrors me; Scripture prizes the friend who sharpens me: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" (Pro 27:17). And choose your twin with care, because you will become like him: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed" (Pro 13:20). The deepest likeness is not to a friend at all. God has predestinated His people "to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren" (Rom 8:29). A father tells his daughter: find friends who look like Christ more than they look like you, and you will grow alike in the best way.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (social-media twinning 2010s; address for a close friend c. 2022–present) for a best friend or kindred spirit — a warm word Scripture deepens from the friend who mirrors me to the friend who sharpens me toward the image of Christ.
webster_full: TWIN, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2022–present; hip-hop and TikTok) A close friend; one who shares your taste, look, or opinion; also a term of address. "Twin, you have to come Saturday."
Twinning, v. and n., dressing or acting alike, often in matching photos. "Twin behaviour" — doing exactly what your friend would do.
The ordinary sense a grandparent knows: one of two children born at one birth, as Jacob and Esau (Gen 25:24).

Webster (1828), root word twin: “TWIN, noun 1. One of two young produced at a birth by an animal that ordinarily brings but one; used mostly in the plural, twins; applied to the young of beasts, as well as to human beings. 2. A sign of the zodiac; Gemini. 3. One very much resembling another.”
Decode for parents: an affectionate term for a best friend; ask who your child’s twin is and what that friend is making them like.
scriptures: And when her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb.
And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
corruption_summary: Twin is a warm word for a friend, which slides easily into prizing the friend who mirrors me over the friend who sharpens me toward Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has real beauty in it. A friend so close you could have shared a birthday is a gift from God, and David found one in Jonathan, whose soul "was knit with the soul of David" (1Sa 18:1). There is nothing wrong with two girls showing up in matching sweaters or two boys finishing each other’s jokes. Scripture celebrates "a friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24), and the slang is closest to grace when it means that.

The drift is toward sameness for its own sake. A friend chosen because he agrees with everything I already think cannot sharpen me; iron does not sharpen iron by matching it, but by striking it (Pro 27:17). The Bible’s actual twins are a warning that likeness of birth is not likeness of heart (Gen 25:24), and its promise points elsewhere: the Father is making a family who all resemble one Brother, Christ, "the firstborn among many brethren" (Rom 8:29). Teach your children to want that likeness above every other, and to pick friends who help them toward it.
roots_summary: Old English twinn (twofold, double) → twin, one of two born together → 2010s twinning (matching) → c. 2022 twin as address for a best friend.
roots_lines: Old English twinn — double, twofold; kin to two and twain
English twin — one of two born at a birth (Gen 25:24)
2010s social media: twinning, matching outfits and poses
c. 2022–2023 hip-hop and TikTok: twin as a term of address for a close friend
usage: "Twin, you literally said what I was thinking."
Iron sharpeneth iron (Pro 27:17) — a good twin sharpens you, not just mirrors you.
The best likeness is to Christ, the firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29).

etymology: From blood as a kinship word. In Black American speech from the 1960s, blood was a term of address for a fellow Black man (it was common among Black soldiers in Vietnam), and in some US cities it was later claimed as a gang greeting. In London the spelling and sound became blud in Multicultural London English (MLE), the youth dialect that grew from Caribbean, African, and Cockney roots in the 1990s–2000s and was spread by grime and UK rap. American Gen Z picked it up c. 2022–2023 through TikTok, especially in the mocking meme format "blud thinks he’s…"
biblical_def: In current slang blud means bro or mate: "you alright, blud?" On American TikTok it is mostly used in the third person to mock someone’s overconfidence: "blud thinks he’s the main character." The word is older and weightier than its users know: it is blood, the kinship of shared birth. The Christian observation: Scripture says both things the word implies, and then says something better. All men are already kin: God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth" (Act 17:26). Kinship brings duty, which is why the first murderer’s sneer, "Am I my brother’s keeper?" (Gen 4:9), is answered by the whole Bible with a yes. Abel’s blood cried from the ground against his brother; but the blood of Jesus, "the blood of sprinkling," "speaketh better things than that of Abel" (Heb 12:24) — it cries mercy, not vengeance. By that blood, strangers "who sometimes were far off are made nigh" (Eph 2:13), and the Son of God, who took our flesh and blood, "is not ashamed to call them brethren" (Heb 2:11). That is the only blood-brotherhood that lasts. A father tells his son: call your friends what you like, but remember that every man you meet is your kin by Adam, and every believer is your brother by the blood of Christ — and treat the second kind as family, because the Lord does.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (from blood, kinship; London MLE 1990s–2000s; US TikTok c. 2022–present) for bro or mate, often in mockery — a word Scripture fills with the one blood of all mankind and the better blood of Christ that makes believers brethren.
webster_full: BLUD, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2022–present in the US; London MLE from the 2000s) Bro, mate, friend; a term of address. "You good, blud?"
US meme use, in the third person, mocking someone’s confidence: "blud thinks he can sing." London pairing: "wagwan, blud" (what’s going on).
Older senses a grandparent will know: blood for kin ("blood is thicker than water"); 1960s–70s Black American blood for a fellow Black man; in some US cities also a gang greeting, so context matters.

Webster (1828), root word blood: “BLOOD, noun 1. The fluid which circulates through the arteries and veins of the human body, and of other animals, which is essential to the preservation of life. This fluid is generally red. If the blood of an animal is not red, such animal is called exsanguious, or white-blooded; the blood being white, or white tinged with blue. 2.”
Decode for parents: mostly a jokey "bro"; in the "blud thinks" format it is a put-down, and the older gang overlay is worth knowing.
scriptures: And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
Gen 4:9
And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?
And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.
Eph 2:13
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
Heb 2:11
For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren,
corruption_summary: Blud borrows the language of blood kinship for casual address and, in its American meme form, for mockery; Scripture keeps the kinship and binds it to the blood of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The word’s root is a true thing. Blood means family, and family means obligation. Cain tried to slip that obligation with a shrug (Gen 4:9), and the ground itself testified against him. Gangs have always borrowed the language of blood for the same reason — it binds — and both the London and the American histories of this word run near that world. In its American TikTok form, blud mostly mocks: "blud thinks he’s him." A word for kin used to belittle a brother is a small picture of Cain.

The gospel takes the word back. Paul told the philosophers of Athens that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men" (Act 17:26) — every human is a relative. And Christ made a nearer kindred by His own blood: those far off are "made nigh by the blood of Christ" (Eph 2:13), and He "is not ashamed to call them brethren" (Heb 2:11). If the Son of God is not ashamed to call us brothers, a Christian boy can learn to use a word like blud without a sneer, and to mean by it something of what Christ means.
roots_summary: Old English blod (blood) → blood as kinship → 1960s Black American address blood → London MLE blud (1990s–2000s) → US TikTok c. 2022.
roots_lines: Old English blod — blood; by extension family, descent, kindred
1960s–70s Black American speech: blood, a fellow Black man
1990s–2000s Multicultural London English, grime, and UK rap: blud, friend or bro
c. 2022–2023 US TikTok: "blud thinks…" mockery memes
usage: "Blud really showed up to the test without a pencil."
God hath made of one blood all nations of men (Act 17:26).
Christ is not ashamed to call His people brethren (Heb 2:11); neither should we be.

etymology: A clipped, London-accented form of brother, with the th sounded as v (as in Cockney bruvver). Bruv is found in British working-class speech from c. the mid-20th century, became a fixture of London youth talk, grime, and road rap in the 2000s, and reached American teens through British memes and TikTok in the 2020s. Unlike blud (from blood), it is plain brother.
biblical_def: In current slang bruv is the British "bro": a friendly, sometimes exasperated address — "cheers, bruv," "bruv, what are you doing?" It is simply brother worn down by a London accent. The Christian observation: brother is one of the great words of the Bible, and a teen who throws it around is handling something precious. "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" (Pro 17:17) — a brother is the one who shows up in the bad week. Christ redrew the family line around obedience: "whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother" (Mat 12:50). The church is therefore a brotherhood in the plain sense, and its rule is "Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another" (Rom 12:10). David sang about what that looks like when it works: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" (Psa 133:1). And Joseph, betrayed and sold by his brothers, met them years later with "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt" (Gen 45:4) — brotherhood restored by forgiveness, a picture of the elder Brother who forgives us. A father tells his son: if you call a boy "bruv," be one — stand with him in adversity, prefer him in honour, and forgive him the way Joseph did.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (British, from brother; London youth speech and grime 2000s; US via memes 2020s) for bro or mate — a worn-down form of one of the Bible’s greatest words, which Christ redefines around doing the Father’s will.
webster_full: BRUV, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present in the US; British, mid-20th c. onward) Brother; bro, mate; a term of address. "Bruv, that’s not how you do it."
Used warmly ("cheers, bruv") or in exasperation ("bruv…"). British cousins: bredren, fam, mate.
Older sense a grandparent will know: brother — a son of the same parents, and in the church a fellow believer.

Webster (1828), root word brother: “BROTHER, noun plural brothers or brethren. […] 1. A human male born of the same father and mother. A male by one of the parents only is called a half-brother, or brother of the half blood. 2. Any one closely united; an associate; as a band of brothers. 3. One that resembles another in manners.”
Decode for parents: friendly British slang for "brother"; clean, and a good door into what Scripture means by brotherhood.
scriptures: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.
Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Gen 45:4
And Joseph said unto his brethren, Come near to me, I pray you. And they came near. And he said, I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt.
corruption_summary: Bruv is clean, friendly slang; the only loss is that a word of covenant weight — brother — is worn smooth into a greeting with no obligation attached.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in bruv itself; it is "brother" in a London accent, and a Christian may use it freely. The thing to watch is what happens to big words when they become small ones. Brother in Scripture is a word of duty: the brother "is born for adversity" (Pro 17:17). He is the one you cannot walk away from. When everyone at the bus stop is "bruv," the word can come to mean only "someone I am not hostile to," and a boy can grow up with plenty of bruvs and no brothers.

Christ restores the weight. He calls His disciples brothers by a stronger tie than blood: "whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother" (Mat 12:50). The church is meant to be the place where that word is true — where brethren "dwell together in unity" (Psa 133:1) and prefer one another in honour (Rom 12:10). Teach your son that a Christian brother is more than a greeting: he is someone you would cross a city for, and forgive the way Joseph forgave (Gen 45:4).
roots_summary: Latin frater / Old English brothor → brother → London bruv (th sounded as v) → grime and road rap (2000s) → US memes and TikTok (2020s).
roots_lines: Old English brothor; Latin frater — a son of the same parents
Cockney and London speech: th sounded as v — bruvver, bruv
Mid-20th c. onward: bruv in British working-class address
2000s grime and road rap: bruv, bredren, fam
2020s: American teens borrow it from British memes and TikTok
usage: "Bruv, you left your hoodie in my car again."
A brother is born for adversity (Pro 17:17) — be one, not just say one.
Whosoever does the will of the Father is Christ’s brother (Mat 12:50).

etymology: American: bro (clipped brother, a common American address since the mid-20th century) plus the affectionate diminutive ending -die, on the pattern of homie and buddy. Brodie spread through hip-hop and Black American speech in the 2010s and became everyday teen address by c. 2018–2020. A grandparent may know an unrelated older word: "to do a Brodie," a reckless leap or a spinning skid, from Steve Brodie, who claimed in 1886 to have jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge.
biblical_def: In current slang brodie is an affectionate "bro": your closest friend, the one you would vouch for — "that’s my brodie, he’s solid." The diminutive makes it warmer than plain bro; it is said with a hand on the shoulder. The Christian observation: the word reaches for something the Bible describes in its finest friendship passages. "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24). Solomon knew that a friend you choose can be truer than kin, and he praised the man who stays: "Thine own friend, and thy father’s friend, forsake not" (Pro 27:10). Friendship needs two because men fall: "if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth" (Ecc 4:10). The Christian reads Proverbs 18:24 and sees Christ, the Friend who stuck closer than any brother when His own brothers did not yet believe Him, and who said to His disciples, "I have called you friends" (Joh 15:15). His friendship is measured in blood: "he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren" (1Jn 3:16). A father tells his son: have a brodie, and be one — the friend who lifts him when he falls, tells him the truth, and would give up his own comfort, even his life, the way Christ gave His for you.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (American bro plus affectionate -die; hip-hop 2010s–present) for a close friend — a warm word the Bible fills with the friend that sticketh closer than a brother, Christ, who laid down His life for His friends.
webster_full: BRODIE, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2015–present; hip-hop and Black American speech) A close friend; an affectionate "bro." "Me and brodie are going to the game."
Used as a name without an article ("brodie said…") or in address ("you good, brodie?"). Also spelled brody; broski is a cousin.
Unrelated older sense a grandparent may know: "to do a Brodie" — a reckless leap or a spinning car skid, after Steve Brodie’s claimed 1886 jump from the Brooklyn Bridge.

Webster (1828), root word brother: “BROTHER, noun plural brothers or brethren. […] 1. A human male born of the same father and mother. A male by one of the parents only is called a half-brother, or brother of the half blood. 2. Any one closely united; an associate; as a band of brothers. 3. One that resembles another in manners.”
Decode for parents: clean and affectionate; it names your child’s closest friend, so learn who brodie is.
scriptures: A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother's house in the day of thy calamity: for better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.
Ecc 4:10
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.
Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.
corruption_summary: Brodie is affectionate and clean; its only weakness is the friendship it often names — loyal to the crew, but not yet the friendship that lays down its life after the pattern of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Teenage boys need friends badly and rarely say so; brodie is one of the ways they say it. That is a good thing. Solomon wrote "woe to him that is alone when he falleth" (Ecc 4:10), and a boy without a brodie is often a boy alone. The question a parent asks is not whether the word is acceptable but what the friendship is made of. Loyalty in the street sense — covering for each other, never telling, backing your boy whether he is right or wrong — is a counterfeit of the real thing.

Scripture shows the real thing. The friend that "sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24) is not the one who covers your sin, but the one who stays when you are low and speaks when you are wrong. Christ is that Friend perfectly. He calls His disciples "friends" (Joh 15:15) and then proves it with a cross, and John draws the line straight to us: "we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren" (1Jn 3:16). Teach your son to be the kind of brodie who would give up his Saturday, his pride, or his reputation for a friend — because his Lord gave up far more.
roots_summary: Old English brothor → brother → American bro → bro plus diminutive -die → brodie in 2010s hip-hop → everyday teen address.
roots_lines: Old English brothor — brother
American bro — clipped address, common from the mid-20th century
Affectionate -ie / -die ending, as in homie, buddy, bestie
2010s hip-hop and Black American speech: brodie, a close friend
Unrelated: Steve Brodie (1886) and the phrase "to do a Brodie"
usage: "Brodie stayed after practice to help me with my jump shot."
There is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother (Pro 18:24) — be that friend.
Christ laid down His life for us; we ought to lay down ours for the brethren (1Jn 3:16).

etymology: From the ordinary sense of a driver pulling up to the curb. Hip-hop used pull up from the 1990s–2000s for arriving somewhere, usually by car and in style, and also as a confrontational dare ("pull up" — come and settle it). By the 2010s it was ordinary teen speech for coming over or showing up ("pull up to my house"), and an invitation by text or social post ("pull up Friday").
biblical_def: In current slang to pull up is to show up: "pull up to the game," "I’ll pull up after work." As an invitation it is warm; as a dare ("pull up, then") it means come and fight. The Christian observation: the Bible is full of invitations to pull up, and the greatest came from Christ. When two disciples asked where He lived, He said, "Come and see" (Joh 1:39), and they stayed with Him that day. He invited Himself to a tax collector’s table — "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house" (Luk 19:5) — and salvation came to that house. The church is the standing pull-up: "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is" (Heb 10:25), and David’s heart leapt at the invitation: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD" (Psa 122:1). Showing up is a real ministry; half of friendship is presence. The dare is another matter. "It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling" (Pro 20:3). A father tells his son: pull up when a friend is hurting, pull up on the Lord’s Day, pull up to the table when you are invited — and when someone says "pull up" to start a fight, the honourable man stays home.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (driving and hip-hop, 1990s–2000s; everyday teen speech 2010s–present) for arriving or showing up, and sometimes a dare to fight — a word Christ fills with "Come and see" and the church with the Lord’s Day assembly.
webster_full: PULL UP, v. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2010–present; hip-hop and car culture) To arrive, come over, or show up somewhere. "Pull up to my house after the game."
As an invitation: "pull up Friday." As a dare or threat: "pull up, then" — come and settle it. Pull-up, n., an arrival or a gathering.
Older senses a grandparent will know: to stop a car or a horse; to rebuke ("pulled him up short"); and the chin-up exercise at the bar.

Webster (1828), root word pull: “PULL, verb transitive […] 1. To draw; to draw towards one or to make an effort to draw. pull differs from draw; we use draw when motion follows the effort, and pull is used in the same sense; but we may also pull forever without drawing or moving the thing. This distinction may not be universal. pull is opposed to push.”
Decode for parents: usually an invitation to come over; said in anger, it is a challenge to fight.
scriptures: Joh 1:39
He saith unto them, Come and see. They came and saw where he dwelt, and abode with him that day: for it was about the tenth hour.
Luk 19:5
And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
A Song of degrees of David. I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.
Pro 20:3
It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling.
corruption_summary: Pull up is mostly a warm invitation to show up, but it doubles as a dare to fight, and the dare is the sense Scripture rejects.
corruption_paragraphs: The good sense of the word is very good. Showing up is most of love: the friend who pulls up to the hospital, the funeral, the moving day, the bad night. Christ’s ministry was a long series of arrivals — at the well, at the tax booth, at the tomb of Lazarus — and His first invitation to disciples was simply "Come and see" (Joh 1:39). The church’s weekly gathering is the same invitation repeated, which is why forsaking it is a sin and not a preference (Heb 10:25).

The other sense needs a firm word. In street and online speech, "pull up" is how a quarrel becomes a fight: a time, a place, a crowd with phones. Boys feel that refusing is cowardice. Scripture calls it honour: "It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling" (Pro 20:3). Courage is not measured by showing up to a fight; it is measured by showing up where love and duty call. Teach your son to be quick to pull up for a friend in need, and to have the backbone to ignore a dare.

etymology: From English link, a ring of a chain. Caribbean, especially Jamaican, speech used link and link up for meeting or connecting with someone; the phrase came into London youth speech (MLE) and UK rap in the 1990s–2000s, and American teens took it up through hip-hop and social media in the 2010s ("let’s link up this weekend"). In British slang a link can also mean a casual romantic contact, a sense parents should know.
biblical_def: In current slang to link up is to meet: "let’s link up after school," "we linked at the mall." It is an ordinary word for an ordinary good — time with friends. In British use a link can also mean a casual romantic partner, which is where a parent should listen closely. The Christian observation: who you link up with is one of the most consequential choices of youth. "Can two walk together, except they be agreed?" (Amo 3:3). Scripture is blunt that company shapes character: "Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners" (1Co 15:33), and "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful" (Psa 1:1) — walking, standing, sitting: the slow slide of a bad link-up. But the Bible also gives the good kind. In Malachi’s dark day, "they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it" (Mal 3:16) — God keeps a book of remembrance of the meetings of His people. The first Christians linked up daily, "breaking bread from house to house" and eating "with gladness and singleness of heart" (Act 2:46). A father tells his daughter: link up often with friends who love the Lord, never link up in secret, and remember that a meeting God hears about is a meeting you should be glad for Him to hear.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (Caribbean and London speech, 1990s–2000s; US teens 2010s–present) for meeting up with someone — an ordinary good whose company shapes character, and which Scripture fills with the fellowship of those that fear the LORD.
webster_full: LINK UP, v. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2010–present in the US; Caribbean and London origin) To meet, hang out, or get together. "We should link up this weekend."
Link, v., the same: "link me later." Link-up, n., a meeting. British a link, n., a casual romantic contact.
Older senses a grandparent will know: a ring of a chain; anything connecting ("the missing link"); to link arms.

Webster (1828), root word link: “LINK, verb transitive 1. To complicate. 2. To unite or connect by something intervening or in other manner. - link towns to towns by avenues of oak. - And creature link'd to creature, man to man.”
Decode for parents: usually just "hang out"; ask where, with whom, and whether "a link" means a friend or a romance.

corruption_summary: Link up is an innocent word for meeting, but it can hide both bad company and the British sense of a casual romance — and Scripture makes company a matter of character.
corruption_paragraphs: Most link-ups are just friends and food, and Christians should have plenty of them. The danger lives in the word’s vagueness. "Linking with some people" can mean a youth group or a party with no parents; and in British slang, which American teens increasingly borrow, "my link" can mean a casual romantic partner kept loose on purpose. Scripture does not let us treat company as neutral: "evil communications corrupt good manners" (1Co 15:33). The first Psalm traces the slide — walking with the ungodly, then standing, then sitting (Psa 1:1).

The remedy is not isolation but better links. Amos asks whether two can walk together except they be agreed (Amo 3:3), and the early church answered by meeting daily, eating in homes, and praising God together (Act 2:46). Malachi records that when the faithful met and talked, "the LORD hearkened, and heard it" (Mal 3:16). Teach your children to link up in the open, with friends who fear God, and to treat any relationship that must be hidden or kept vague as a warning light.
